One: its meaning is that the matter became clear and manifest, and the Arabs use it as a proverb for what has become clear. The poet said:

؎ أقِيمُوا بَنِي أُمِّي صُدُورَ مَطِيِّكم ∗∗∗ فَإنِّي إلى قَوْمٍ سِواكم لَأمْيَلُ ∗∗∗ فَقَدْ حَمَّتِ الحاجاتُ واللَّيْلُ مُقْمِرُ ∗∗∗ وشُدِّتْ لِطَيّاتٍ مَطايا وأرْحَلُ

(Aqimū banī ummī ṣudūra maṭiyyikum, fa-innī ila qawmin siwākum la-amyalu, faqad ḥammat al-ḥājātu wal-laylu muqmiru, wa shuddat li-ṭayyātin maṭāyā wa arḥalu.)

Second: that the splitting of the moon is the splitting of darkness away from it by its rising in the midst of it, just as dawn is called "falaq" (a cleaving) because darkness is cleft away from it; and its cleaving may be expressed by "inshiqaq" (splitting), as al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

(Falamma adbarū wa lahum dawiyyun, da'ānā 'inda shaqqi al-ṣubḥi dā'ī.)

One: that He meant, whatever sign they see, they turn away from it and do not take heed from it; and for this reason He mentioned it in indefinite form rather than definite. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Two: that by "the sign" He meant the splitting of the moon when they saw it.

One: that the meaning of "mustamirr" is "passing away" (dhahib). This was said by Anas and Abu 'Ubaydah.

Two: "strong," taken from "imrar al-habl" (twisting a rope), which is the intensity of its twisting. This was said by al-Akhfash and al-Farra'.

Three: that it resembles one part of it to another.

Four: that "mustamirr" means "lasting," and Imru' al-Qays said:

One: the Day of Resurrection.

Two: every matter is settled in that good belongs to the people of good and evil to the people of evil. This was said by Qatadah.

Three: that every matter is settled, its truth distinguished from its falsehood.

Four: that everything has an end and a limit in its occurrence and its arrival. This was said by al-Suddi.

It may also admit a fifth: that it means the enduring of the reward of the believer and the punishment of the disbeliever.

﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news﴾. On this there are two views:

One: the narratives of the former nations. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Two: the Qur'an.

﴿In which is a deterrent﴾: that is, a preventer from sins.

It may admit two views:

One: that it is the prohibition.

Two: that it is the threat.

One: far-reaching in admonishing you.

(Qad iqtarabat law kana fi qurbi darihā jidā'un, wa lakin qad taḍurru wa tanfa'u.)

By "the Hour" is meant the Resurrection. Regarding its being called "the Hour" there are two explanations:

First: because of the swiftness of the matter in it.

Second: because it comes at an hour of its day.

Tariq ibn Shihab narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour has drawn near, and people increase in nothing in regard to this world except greed, and it increases in nothing from them except distance."

﴿And the moon has split﴾. On this there are three opinions:

One: its meaning is that the matter became clear and manifest, and the Arabs use it as a proverb for what has become clear. The poet said:

؎ أقِيمُوا بَنِي أُمِّي صُدُورَ مَطِيِّكم ∗∗∗ فَإنِّي إلى قَوْمٍ سِواكم لَأمْيَلُ ∗∗∗ فَقَدْ حَمَّتِ الحاجاتُ واللَّيْلُ مُقْمِرُ ∗∗∗ وشُدِّتْ لِطَيّاتٍ مَطايا وأرْحَلُ

(Aqimū banī ummī ṣudūra maṭiyyikum, fa-innī ila qawmin siwākum la-amyalu, faqad ḥammat al-ḥājātu wal-laylu muqmiru, wa shuddat li-ṭayyātin maṭāyā wa arḥalu.)

Second: that the splitting of the moon is the splitting of darkness away from it by its rising in the midst of it, just as dawn is called "falaq" (a cleaving) because darkness is cleft away from it; and its cleaving may be expressed by "inshiqaq" (splitting), as al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

؎ فَلَمّا أدْبَرُوا ولَهم دَوِيٌّ ∗∗∗ دَعانا عِنْدَ شَقِّ الصُّبْحِ داعِي

(Falamma adbarū wa lahum dawiyyun, da'ānā 'inda shaqqi al-ṣubḥi dā'ī.)

Third: that it is the splitting of the moon in its literal reality.

Regarding this interpretation there are two views:

One: that it will split after the coming of the Hour, which is the second blast. This is the view of al-Hasan, who said: "For if it split, no one would remain who did not see it, since it is a sign, and people are equal regarding signs."

Two: and this is the view of the majority and the apparent sense of the revelation, that the moon split during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), after his uncle Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, when he embraced Islam out of anger at Abu Jahl's insult to the Messenger of Allah, asked him to show him a sign by which he would increase in certainty in his faith. Mujahid narrated from Abu Ma'mar, from Abu Mas'ud, who said: "I saw the moon split into two halves in Makkah before the Prophet (ﷺ) migrated to Madinah: one half over Abu Qubays and one half over al-Suwayda'. They said, 'Magic has bewitched the moon,' and then this was revealed: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾."

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾. On this there are two views:

One: that He meant, whatever sign they see, they turn away from it and do not take heed from it; and for this reason He mentioned it in indefinite form rather than definite. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Two: that by "the sign" He meant the splitting of the moon when they saw it.

﴿And they say, "Enduring magic"﴾. On this there are five views:

One: that the meaning of "mustamirr" is "passing away" (dhahib). This was said by Anas and Abu 'Ubaydah.

Two: "strong," taken from "imrar al-habl" (twisting a rope), which is the intensity of its twisting. This was said by al-Akhfash and al-Farra'.

Three: that it resembles one part of it to another.

Four: that "mustamirr" means "lasting," and Imru' al-Qays said:

؎ ألا إنَّما الدُّنْيا لَيالٍ وأعْصُرَ ∗∗∗ ولَيْسَ عَلى شَيْءٍ قَوِيمٍ بِمُسْتَمِرٍّ

(Alā innamā al-dunyā layālin wa a'ṣura, wa laysa 'alā shay'in qawīmin bimustamirri.)

That is, with something lasting.

Five: that is, it has extended from the earth to the sky. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿And every matter is settled﴾. On this there are four views:

One: the Day of Resurrection.

Two: every matter is settled in that good belongs to the people of good and evil to the people of evil. This was said by Qatadah.

Three: that every matter is settled, its truth distinguished from its falsehood.

Four: that everything has an end and a limit in its occurrence and its arrival. This was said by al-Suddi.

It may also admit a fifth: that it means the enduring of the reward of the believer and the punishment of the disbeliever.

﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news﴾. On this there are two views:

One: the narratives of the former nations. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Two: the Qur'an.

﴿In which is a deterrent﴾: that is, a preventer from sins.

It may admit two views:

One: that it is the prohibition.

Two: that it is the threat.

﴿Far-reaching wisdom﴾. Al-Suddi said: it is the message and the Book.

(p-411) It may also be that it refers to the promise and the threat.

The phrase ﴿bāligha﴾ may admit two views:

One: far-reaching in admonishing you.

Two: reaching from Allah to you. So on the first view it is from intensification (mubalagha), and on the second it is from conveying (iblagh).

﴿Then of what use are warnings?﴾ That is: what prevents them from denial is not the warning.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 54, verses 6–8:

﴿Hastening toward the Caller﴾. Regarding this, there are six interpretations.

The first: its meaning is "hastening," said by Abu 'Ubayda (Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna). From it is the saying of the poet:

Bi-Dijla dārahum, wa-laqad arāhum
Bi-Dijla muhṭi'īna ila al-samā'
(In the Tigris is their dwelling, and indeed I saw them in the Tigris, hastening toward the sound of the singing.)

The second: its meaning is "approaching," said by al-Dahhak.

The third: "intending," said by Qatada.

The fourth: "looking," said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fifth: "stretching out their ears toward the sound," said by 'Ikrima.

The sixth: "lowering their gaze between their eyes" (i.e., fixing their eyes downward), said by Tamim.

﴿The disbelievers will say, "This is a difficult day"﴾. He means the Day of Resurrection, because of the hardship they will suffer on it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 54, verse 18–22:

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind﴾ (rīḥan ṣarṣaran). Regarding it there are three interpretations:

First: it means cold. This is said by Qatadah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Second: it means violently blowing. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

Third: it is the wind whose blowing is heard like a sound (ṣawt). From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ A falcon crying out (yuṣarṣiru) atop the high watchtower

﴿On a day of ill omen, continuous﴾ (fī yawmi naḥsin mustamirrin). Regarding it there are three interpretations:

First: it was a day of punishment and destruction.

Second: it was called so because it was a Wednesday (yawm al-arbaʿāʾ).

Third: it was called so because it was a cold day. Al-Shanfarā said:

؎ And a night of ill omen, its owner warming himself by the bow, and by the arrows with which he shoots (yanbulu)

He means that because of its intense cold, he warms himself with his bow and his arrows, with which he defends himself.

Regarding ﴿mustamirr﴾ (continuous) there are two interpretations:

First: it means passing away (al-dhāhib).

Second: it means lasting (al-dāʾim).

On this interpretation, there are two aspects to their saying that:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّهم قالُوهُ لِعِظَمِ ما نالَهم أنْ يَتْبَعُوا رَجُلًا واحِدًا مِنهم، كَما يَقُولُ الرَّجُلُ إذا نالَهُ خَطْبٌ عَظِيمٌ: أنا في النّارِ.

The second: when they were threatened with the fire for denying him and opposing him, they returned the same words that had been said to them, saying: "If we follow one man like ourselves, then we would indeed be in error and in the fire."

﴿بَلْ هو كَذّابٌ أشِرٌ﴾ فِيهِ ثَلاثَةُ أقاوِيلَ:

﴿Rather, he is a great liar, insolent﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

أحَدُها: أنَّ الأشِرَ هو العَظِيمُ الكَذِبِ، قالَهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

The first: *ashir* (أشِر) is one who is greatly given to lying. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: that it means *battir* (بَطِر), the wanton and arrogant one. From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ أشَرْتُمْ بِلِبْسِ الخَزِّ لَمّا لَبِسْتُمْ ومِن قَبْلُ لا تَدْرُونَ مَن فَتَحَ القُرى

*You became insolent by wearing silk brocade, when you put it on, while before that you did not even know who conquered the towns.*

الثّالِثُ: أنَّهُ المُتَعَدِّي إلى مَنزِلَةٍ لا يَسْتَحِقُّها.

The third: that he is one who overreaches to a rank he does not deserve.

﴿إنّا مُرْسِلُو النّاقَةِ فِتْنَةً لَهم فارْتَقِبْهم واصْطَبِرْ﴾ أمّا الِاصْطِبارُ فَهو الِافْتِعالُ مِنَ الصَّبْرِ وأصْلُ الطّاءِ تاءٌ أُبْدِلَتْ بِطاءٍ لِيَكُونَ اللَّفْظُ أسْهَلُ مَخْرَجًا ويَعْذُبُ مَسْمَعًا.

﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel as a trial for them, so watch them and be patient﴾. Its original root letter is the *ta'* (تاءٌ), which was replaced by a *ta'* (طاءٌ) so that the word would be easier to pronounce and more pleasant to hear.

The second: the Thamud would come to the water on her off day and drink, and they would come for the milk on her day of coming and milk her.

*Or after him, like Qidar, when peoples followed him in his misguided deed, and then they perished.*

﴿Then he took (it)﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: its meaning is that he seized it with his hand. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

الثّانِي: مَعْناهُ تَناوَلَها وأخَذَها، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ حَسّانِ بْنِ ثابِتٍ

The second: its meaning is that he reached for it and took hold of it. From this is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

*Both of them milked the juice, then handed me, in a flask, the one that loosened them for the mufassal.*

*It raised a cloud of dust like the smoke of a fire, kindled in a decayed, crushed gharqad (thorn tree).*

*You see the carcasses of mounts on both its sides, as if their bones were the wood of dry debris.*

الثّانِي: العَناءُ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ.

الثّالِثُ: الِافْتِراقُ، قالَهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

أحَدُها: أنَّ السُّعُرَ الجُنُونُ، قالَهُ ابْنُ كامِلٍ.

الثّانِي: العَناءُ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ.

The second: *al-'anaa'* (hardship, toil). This was said by Qatadah.

الثّالِثُ: الِافْتِراقُ، قالَهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

The third: separation (divergence). This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: bewilderment (going astray). This was said by al-Dahhak.

وَعَلى هَذا التَّأْوِيلِ في قَوْلِهِمْ ذَلِكَ وجْهانِ:

On this interpretation, there are two aspects to their saying that:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّهم قالُوهُ لِعِظَمِ ما نالَهم أنْ يَتْبَعُوا رَجُلًا واحِدًا مِنهم، كَما يَقُولُ الرَّجُلُ إذا نالَهُ خَطْبٌ عَظِيمٌ: أنا في النّارِ.

The first: they said it because of the great harm it would bring upon them to follow one man from among themselves, just as a man says when a great calamity befalls him: "I am in the fire."

الثّانِي: أنَّهم لَمّا أُوعِدُوا عَلى تَكْذِيبِهِ ومُخالَفَتِهِ بِالنّارِ رَدُّوا مِثْلَ ما قِيلَ لَهم إنّا لَوِ اتَّبَعْنا رَجُلًا مِثْلَنا واحِدًا كُنّا إذًا في النّارِ.

The second: when they were threatened with the fire for denying him and opposing him, they returned the same words that had been said to them, saying: "If we follow one man like ourselves, then we would indeed be in error and in the fire."

﴿بَلْ هو كَذّابٌ أشِرٌ﴾ فِيهِ ثَلاثَةُ أقاوِيلَ:

﴿Rather, he is a great liar, insolent﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

أحَدُها: أنَّ الأشِرَ هو العَظِيمُ الكَذِبِ، قالَهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

The first: *ashir* (أشِر) is one who is greatly given to lying. This was said by al-Suddi.

الثّانِي: أنَّهُ البَطِرُ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ الشّاعِرِ

The second: that it means *battir* (بَطِر), the wanton and arrogant one. From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ أشَرْتُمْ بِلِبْسِ الخَزِّ لَمّا لَبِسْتُمْ ومِن قَبْلُ لا تَدْرُونَ مَن فَتَحَ القُرى

*You became insolent by wearing silk brocade, when you put it on, while before that you did not even know who conquered the towns.*

The third: that he is one who overreaches to a rank he does not deserve.

The first: the she-camel would be present at the water on their day of coming, and absent from them on her day of coming. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: the Thamud would come to the water on her off day and drink, and they would come for the milk on her day of coming and milk her.

﴿So they called their companion﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ أحْمَرُ إرَمَ وشَقِيُها، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ، وقَدْ ذَكَرَهُ زُهَيْرٌ في شِعْرِهِ فَقالَ

The first: he is the red one of Iram, and the wretched one among them. This was said by Qatadah, and Zuhayr mentioned him in his poetry, saying:

*So she bears for you boys, all of them ill-omened, like the red one of 'Ad; then she suckles and weans.*

The second: he is Qadar ibn Salif. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, and al-Afwah mentioned him in his poetry:

*Or after him, like Qidar, when peoples followed him in his misguided deed, and then they perished.*

﴿Then he took (it)﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّ مَعْناهُ بَطَشَ بِيَدِهِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ.

The first: its meaning is that he seized it with his hand. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: its meaning is that he reached for it and took hold of it. From this is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

*Both of them milked the juice, then handed me, in a flask, the one that loosened them for the mufassal.*

﴿Then he hamstrung﴾ (*'aqara*). Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Qidar lay in wait for her in the root of a tree on her path, shot her with an arrow which lodged in the muscle of her leg, then he attacked her with the sword and cut her hamstring. She fell and let out a single cry, and her young one dropped from her belly and ran until it reached a rock at the top of the mountain, where it cried out and took refuge there. Then Salih came to them, and when he saw that they had hamstrung the she-camel, he wept and said: "You have violated the sanctity of Allah, so rejoice in the punishment of Allah."

﴿So they became like the crushed debris of the one who builds an enclosure﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions:

*It raised a cloud of dust like the smoke of a fire, kindled in a decayed, crushed gharqad (thorn tree).*

(p-٤١٦)وَفِيهِ وجْهانِ:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّ النّاقَةَ تَحْضُرُ الماءَ يَوْمَ وُرُودِهِمْ، وتَغِيبُ عَنْهم يَوْمَ وُرُودِها، قالَهُ مُقاتِلٌ.

؎ أثْرَتْ عُجاجَةً كَدُخانِ نارٍ ∗∗∗ تَشِبُّ بِغَرْقَدٍ بالٍ هَشِيمِ

*It raised a cloud of dust like the smoke of a fire, kindled in a decayed, crushed gharqad (thorn tree).*

This was said by al-Dahhak.

*You see the carcasses of mounts on both its sides, as if their bones were the wood of dry debris.*

أحَدُها: أنَّ السُّعُرَ الجُنُونُ، قالَهُ ابْنُ كامِلٍ.

The first: *su'ur* (السُّعُر) means madness. This was said by Ibn Kamil.

الثّانِي: العَناءُ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ.

The second: *al-'anaa'* (hardship, toil). This was said by Qatadah.

الثّالِثُ: الِافْتِراقُ، قالَهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

The third: separation (divergence). This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: bewilderment (going astray). This was said by al-Dahhak.

أحَدُها: أنَّ الأشِرَ هو العَظِيمُ الكَذِبِ، قالَهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

The first: *ashir* (أشِر) is one who is greatly given to lying. This was said by al-Suddi.

الثّانِي: أنَّهُ البَطِرُ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ الشّاعِرِ

*You became insolent by wearing silk brocade, when you put it on, while before that you did not even know who conquered the towns.*

*It raised a cloud of dust like the smoke of a fire, kindled in a decayed, crushed gharqad (thorn tree).*

﴿Rather, he is a great liar, insolent﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

*You became insolent by wearing silk brocade, when you put it on, while before that you did not even know who conquered the towns.*

أحَدُهُما: أنَّ النّاقَةَ تَحْضُرُ الماءَ يَوْمَ وُرُودِهِمْ، وتَغِيبُ عَنْهم يَوْمَ وُرُودِها، قالَهُ مُقاتِلٌ.

The first: the she-camel would be present at the water on their day of coming, and absent from them on her day of coming. This was said by Muqatil.

الثّانِي: أنَّ ثَمُودَ يَحْضُرُونَ الماءَ يَوْمَ غِبِّها فَيَشْرَبُونَ، ويَحْضُرُونَ اللَّبَنَ يَوْمَ ورْدِها فَيَحْلِبُونَ.

The second: the Thamud would come to the water on her off day and drink, and they would come for the milk on her day of coming and milk her.

﴿فَنادَوْا صاحِبَهُمْ﴾ فِيهِ قَوْلانِ:

﴿So they called their companion﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ أحْمَرُ إرَمَ وشَقِيُها، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ، وقَدْ ذَكَرَهُ زُهَيْرٌ في شِعْرِهِ فَقالَ

The first: he is the red one of Iram, and the wretched one among them. This was said by Qatadah, and Zuhayr mentioned him in his poetry, saying:

؎ فَتَنْتُجُ لَكم غِلْمانَ أشْأمَ كُلَّهم ∗∗∗ كَأحْمَرِ عادٍ ثُمَّ تُرْضِعُ فَتَفْطِمُ

*So she bears for you boys, all of them ill-omened, like the red one of 'Ad; then she suckles and weans.*

الثّانِي: أنَّهُ قَدارُ بْنُ سالِفٍ، قالَهُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ إسْحاقَ، وقَدْ ذَكَرَهُ الأفْوَهُ في شِعْرِهِ

The second: he is Qadar ibn Salif. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, and al-Afwah mentioned him in his poetry:

؎ أوْ بَعْدَهُ كَقِدارٍ حِينَ تابَعَهُ ∗∗∗ عَلى الغاوِيَةِ أقْوامٌ فَقَدْ بادُوا

*Or after him, like Qidar, when peoples followed him in his misguided deed, and then they perished.*

﴿فَتَعاطى﴾ فِيهِ وجْهانِ:

﴿Then he took (it)﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّ مَعْناهُ بَطَشَ بِيَدِهِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ.

The first: its meaning is that he seized it with his hand. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

الثّانِي: مَعْناهُ تَناوَلَها وأخَذَها، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ حَسّانِ بْنِ ثابِتٍ

The second: its meaning is that he reached for it and took hold of it. From this is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

؎ كِلْتاهُما حَلَبَ العَصِيرَ فَعاطَنِي ∗∗∗ بِزُجاجَةٍ أرْخاهُما لِلْمُفَصَّلِ

*Both of them milked the juice, then handed me, in a flask, the one that loosened them for the mufassal.*

﴿فَعَقَرَ﴾ قالَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ إسْحاقَ: كَمَن لَها قِدارٌ في أصْلِ شَجَرَةٍ عَلى طَرِيقِها فَرَماها بِسَهْمٍ فانْتَظَمَ بِهِ عَضَلَةُ ساقِها، ثُمَّ شَدَّ عَلَيْها بِالسَّيْفِ فَكَشَفَ عُرْقُوبَها فَخَرَّتْ ورَغَتْ رُغاءَةً واحِدَةً تَحَدَّرَ سُقْبُها [مِن بَطْنِها وانْطَلَقَ سُقْبُها] حَتّى أتى صَخْرَةً في رَأْسِ الجَبَلِ فَرَغا ثُمَّ لاذَ بِها، فَأتاهم صالِحٌ، فَلَمّا رَأى النّاقَةَ قَدْ عَقَرُوها بَكى ثُمَّ قالَ: انْتَهَكْتُمْ حُرْمَةَ اللَّهِ فَأبْشِرُوا بِعَذابِ اللَّهِ.

﴿Then he hamstrung﴾ (*'aqara*). Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Qidar lay in wait for her in the root of a tree on her path, shot her with an arrow which lodged in the muscle of her leg, then he attacked her with the sword and cut her hamstring. She fell and let out a single cry, and her young one dropped from her belly and ran until it reached a rock at the top of the mountain, where it cried out and took refuge there. Then Salih came to them, and when he saw that they had hamstrung the she-camel, he wept and said: "You have violated the sanctity of Allah, so rejoice in the punishment of Allah."

قالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ: وكانَ الَّذِي عَقَرَها رَجُلٌ أحْمَرُ أزْرَقُ أشْقَرُ أكْشَفُ أقْفى.

Ibn Abbas said: The one who hamstrung her was a man who was red-faced, blue-eyed, reddish-haired, with a receding hairline and a flat back of the head.

﴿فَكانُوا كَهَشِيمِ المُحْتَظِرِ﴾ فِيهِ خَمْسَةُ أقاوِيلَ:

﴿So they became like the crushed debris of the one who builds an enclosure﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions:

أحَدُهُما: يَعْنِي العِظامَ المُحْتَرِقَةَ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ.

The first: it means the burnt bones. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

(p-٤١٧)الثّانِي: أنَّهُ التُّرابُ الَّذِي يَتَناثَرُ مِنَ الحائِطِ وتُصِيبُهُ الرِّيحُ، فَيَحْتَظِرُ مُسْتَدِيرًا، قالَهُ سَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ.

The second: it is the dust that scatters from a wall and is struck by the wind, so that it forms a circle around itself. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

الثّالِثُ: أنَّها الحِظارُ البالِيَةُ مِنَ الخَشَبِ إذا صارَ هَشِيمًا، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ الشّاعِرِ

The third: they are the decayed enclosures of wood when they have become crushed debris. From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ أثْرَتْ عُجاجَةً كَدُخانِ نارٍ ∗∗∗ تَشِبُّ بِغَرْقَدٍ بالٍ هَشِيمِ

*It raised a cloud of dust like the smoke of a fire, kindled in a decayed, crushed gharqad (thorn tree).*

قالَهُ الضَّحّاكُ.

This was said by al-Dahhak.

الرّابِعُ: أنَّهُ حَشِيشٌ قَدْ حَظَرَتْهُ الغَنَمُ فَأكَلَتْهُ، وهو مَرْوِيٌّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ أيْضًا

The fourth: it is grass that the sheep have enclosed and then eaten. This is also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

الخامِسُ: أنَّ الهَشِيمَ اليابِسَ مِنَ الشَّجَرِ الَّذِي فِيهِ شَوْكٌ والمُحْتَظِرُ الَّذِي تَحْظُرُ بِهِ العَرَبُ حَوْلَ ماشِيَتِها مِنَ السِّباعِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ زَيْدٍ، وقالَ الشّاعِرُ

The fifth: the *hashim* (هَشِيم) is the dry, thorny wood of trees, and the *muhtazir* (مُحْتَظِر) is that with which the Arabs fence around their livestock against predators. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and the poet said:

؎ تَرى جِيَفَ المَطِيِّ بِجانِبَيْهِ ∗∗∗ كَأنَّ عِظامُها خَشَبَ الهَشِيمِ.

*You see the carcasses of mounts on both its sides, as if their bones were the wood of dry debris.*

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 54, verses 33–40:

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind carrying pebbles﴾ Regarding this there are five interpretations:

First: that al-hasb (the pebbles) are the stones with which they were pelted from the sky, and al-hasba' (the gravel) is pebbles and small stones.

Second: that al-hasib (the one carrying pebbles) is the pelting with stones and other things, and for this reason the Arabs call whatever the wind blows about "hasiban." Al-Farazdaq said:

Facing the north of Syria, it strikes us with a hasib like scattered cotton fluff.

Third: that al-hasib is the cloud that pelted them.

(p-418) Fourth: that al-hasib is the angels who pelted them.

Fifth: that al-hasib is the wind that bore the gravel upon them.

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾ meaning his son and those who believed in him.

﴿We saved them at dawn﴾. Al-sahar (the pre-dawn) is the period between the last part of the night and the rising of dawn. In the language of the Arabs it is the mingling of the darkness of the last part of the night with the whiteness of the beginning of the day, because at this time there are the signs (makhayil) of the night and the signs of the day.

﴿And they had already sought to seduce him from his guests﴾, meaning Lot's guests, who were the angels that descended upon him in the form of men, and they were in their most beautiful forms. So they sought to seduce Lot regarding them, desiring the vile deed.

﴿So We obliterated their eyes﴾. Al-tamս (obliteration) is the erasing of a trace, and from it comes "the book was obliterated" when it is erased. Regarding the obliteration of their eyes there are two views:

One: that they were concealed from their sight so that they did not see them, while their eyes remained intact. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Second: their eyes were obliterated until their sight was gone and they became blind, so they did not see them. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿So taste My punishment and warnings﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

One: that it is a threat of the lesser punishment. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Second: that it is a rebuke with what befell them of the punishment of blindness that descended upon them. This is the meaning of the statement of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 54, verse 47–55:

﴿Indeed, We have created all things by decree (qadar).﴾ Isma'il ibn Ziyad narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Abbad, from Abu Hurayrah, that: "The polytheists of Quraysh came to the Prophet (ﷺ) disputing with him about qadar, and so this was revealed."

﴿Indeed, We have created all things by decree.﴾ On this there are two views:

The first: according to the measure of what We willed, without increase or decrease. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: by a prior judgment and a decree that is binding. From this is the words of the rajaz poet:

"And the decree of the Decreer, the decrees."

﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye.﴾ It means that whatever We will of a thing, We command it once, and We do not need a second time for it. So that thing, along with Our command to it, is like the blink of an eye in its swiftness, without delay or postponement.

﴿And every small and great thing is recorded (mustatar).﴾ On this there are two views:

The first: that al-mustatar means "the written," said by al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd, because it is inscribed (mastur).

The second: that it means "the preserved," said by Qatadah.

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and a river (nahar).﴾ On this there are three views:

The first: that nahar means rivers of water, wine, honey and milk. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The second: that nahar means light and illumination, and from it comes the word "daytime" (nahar). This was said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, and from it is the words of the rajaz poet:

"Were it not for the two thriddahs, we would have perished from hunger: the thrid of the night and the thrid of the nahar."

The third: that it means abundance of living and great bounty, and from it comes the name of a river of water. This was said by Qutrub.

(p-421) ﴿In a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent.﴾ On this there are two views:

The first: a seat of truth, in which there is no idle talk and no sin.

The second: a seat of truth belonging to God, which He promised to His friends. Al-Malik and al-Malik are one and the same, and He is God, as Ibn al-Zib'ari said:

"O Messenger of the Sovereign, indeed my tongue is a mender of what I have torn when they repent."

It may also bear a third meaning: that al-Malik is the one deserving of sovereignty, and al-Malik is the one who establishes sovereignty, and al-Muqtadir means al-Qadir (the Able).

Regarding God's describing Himself here with power (iqtidar), there are two possible views:

The first: to magnify the status of those among the righteous who are with Him, for they are of greater worth and higher rank in the presence of the Omnipotent.

The second: so that they may know that He is able to preserve for them the blessings He has bestowed upon them and to make them lasting for them. And God knows best.
